--- title: "Part 4. Building a DES Progressive Disease Model" format: closeread-html: css: des-styling.css code-tools: false fig-format: svg toc: false linkcolor: tomato bibliography: references.bib editor_options: chunk_output_type: console editor: source --- ::: {.cell} ::: :::{.cr-section} @cr-petrisick Our next objective is to build in a single [**sick**]{style="color:crimson"} health state. :::{#cr-petrisick} ![](images/petri-model4.png){fig-align="center"} ::: [@cr-petrisick]{pan-to="90%, 50%" scale-by="2.8"} Notice that the sick state will allow for disease recovery (i.e., a return to the [**Healthy**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"} state). [@cr-petrisick]{pan-to="90%, 50%" scale-by="2.8"} We therefore need to add in two new transitions: (1) becoming ill; and (2) disease recovery. @cr-inputs2 Let's now re-define the model inputs. [@cr-inputs2]{highlight="6"} We include an annual hazard rate of progression from [**Healthy**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"} to [**Sick**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"}. [@cr-inputs2]{highlight="7"} As well as an annual disease recovery rate. [@cr-inputs2]{highlight="8"} The hazard rate of death from Healthy remains the same. [@cr-inputs2]{highlight="9"} But patients in the sick state have a higher rate of death, as summarized by a hazard ratio. [@cr-inputs2]{highlight="11-15"} Later we'll build in some accounting of costs and quality of life, so we include cost and QALY parameters in the inputs as well. [@cr-inputs2]{highlight="18"} We'll also cover point and interval discounting when we come to outcome estimation. :::{#cr-inputs2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} inputs <- list( N = 1, # Total number of patients to simulate. horizon = 110, # Time horizon (years) min_age = 20, max_age = 30, r.HS1 = 0.15, # Disease Onset Rate / year (H -> S) r.S1H = 0.7, # Recovery Rate / year (S -> H) r.HD = 0.005, # Healthy to Dead rate / year (H -> D) hr.S1D = 3, # Hazard ratio in S1 vs healthy c.H = 2000, # Healthy individuals c.S1 = 4000, # Sick individuals in S1 u.H = 1.00, # Healthy u.S1 = 0.80, # S1 # Cycle => 1 year d.r = 0.03 # Discount Rate ) ``` ::: ::: [@cr-initialize]{highlight="1-6"} Let's add the sick state to the counters. [@cr-initialize]{highlight="5"} Note that we index sick with a value of 1. That's because **simmer** requires that health states be tracked using a numeric categorical variable that starts with zero. [@cr-initialize]{highlight="8-16"} We next add code initilise all patients into the healthy state. [@cr-initialize]{highlight="14"} We do this be setting the `state` attribute value to zero upon inilialisation of the patient. [@cr-initialize]{highlight="15"} We'll also want to track the amount of time spent in the healthy state later, for estimation of quality-of-life. So we need to add time in the [**healthy**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"} state to our resource counters. :::{#cr-initialize} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} counters <- c( "time_in_model", "death", "healthy", "sick1" ) # Define starting state of patient initialize_patient <- function(traj, inputs) { traj |> seize("time_in_model") |> set_attribute("AgeInitial", function() sample(20:30, 1)) |> set_attribute("State", 0) |> # Patients start healthy seize("healthy") } ``` ::: ::: @cr-deathevent2 Because the death rate now depends on health state, we amend our `time_to_death` function to draw a death time depending on whether the patient is [**Healthy**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"} or [**Sick**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"}. :::{#cr-deathevent2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} years_till_death <- function(inputs) { state <- get_attribute(env, "State") rate <- inputs$r.HD if(state == 1) rate <- rate * inputs$hr.S1D # Deal with Sick1 Hazard Ratio rexp(1, rate) } ``` ::: ::: @cr-sickevent2 The function that draws years till sick uses a draw from the exponential distribution, and only sets a value within the simulation time horizon if the patient is in the [**healthy**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"} state. :::{#cr-sickevent2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} years_till_sick1 <- function(inputs) { state <- get_attribute(env, "State") if(state == 0) # 0 => Healthy { rexp(1,inputs$r.HS1) } else { inputs$horizon+1 # Past end of simulation time } } ``` ::: ::: @cr-sickevent2b Once the patient transitions into the **sick** state, we reset her state attribute to a value of 1 (i.e., sick). [@cr-sickevent2b]{highlight="5,6"} She also releases the `healthy` resource and seizes the `sick` resouce. Again, this facilitates tracking total amount of time in each health state. :::{#cr-sickevent2b} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} sick1 <- function(traj, inputs) { traj |> set_attribute("State", 1) |> # 1 => Sick 1 (S1) release('healthy') |> # Track state change for tally later seize('sick1') } ``` ::: ::: [@cr-petrisick]{pan-to="90%, 60%" scale-by="2.8"} Recall that in this model, patients can recover and become healthy again. @cr-healthy2 To allow for this, we need to define a function for **time to healthy** and a function that releases the [**sick**]{style="color:#79AF97FF"} resource and re-seizes [**healthy**]{style="color:#79AF97FF"}. :::{#cr-healthy2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} years_till_healthy <- function(inputs) { state <- get_attribute(env, "State") if(state == 1) # 1 => Sick 1 { rexp(1,inputs$r.S1H) } else { inputs$horizon+1 # Past end of simulation time } } healthy <- function(traj, inputs) { traj |> set_attribute("State", 0) |> # 0 => Healthy (H) seize('healthy') |> release('sick1') } ``` ::: ::: @cr-cleanup2 We need to also amend our **cleanup** function so that it releases the [**healthy**]{style="color:#79AF97FF"} resource (if healthy) and [**sick**]{style="color:#79AF97FF"} resource (if sick) at the termination of the model. :::{#cr-cleanup2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} cleanup_on_termination <- function(traj) { traj |> release("time_in_model") |> branch( function() get_attribute(env, "State")+1, continue = rep(TRUE, 3), trajectory() |> release("healthy"), trajectory() |> release("sick1"), trajectory() ) } ``` ::: ::: @cr-registry2 Finally, we amend our **event registry** so that our model output records events for becoming ill and healthy. :::{#cr-registry2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} event_registry <- list( list(name = "Terminate at time horizon", attr = "aTerminate", time_to_event = function(inputs) inputs$horizon-now(env), func = terminate_simulation, reactive = FALSE), list(name = "Death", attr = "aDeath", time_to_event = years_till_death, func = death, reactive = TRUE), list(name = "Sick1", attr = "aSick1", time_to_event = years_till_sick1, func = sick1, reactive = TRUE), list(name = "Healthy", attr = "aHealthy", time_to_event = years_till_healthy, func = healthy, reactive = TRUE) ) ``` ::: ::: @cr-Rmodel2resultrun Our `des_run()` function does not need to be amended because we took care of all the changes in the other model functions. :::{#cr-Rmodel2resultrun} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} des_run <- function(inputs) { env <<- simmer("SickSicker") traj <- des(env, inputs) env |> create_counters(counters) |> add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, inputs$N)), mon=2) |> run(inputs$horizon+1/365) |> # Simulate just past horizon (in years) wrap() get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T) } set.seed(1) res_model <- des_run(inputs) ``` ::: ::: @cr-Rmodel2result This table (from the `res_model` object) shows a partial trajectory for a single patient. We can see that the patient bounces back and forth between the [**healthy**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"} and [**sick**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"} health states. :::{#cr-Rmodel2result} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |name |start_time |end_time |activity_time |resource | |:--------|:----------|:--------|:-------------|:--------| |patient2 |0 |11.99 |11.99 |healthy | |patient2 |11.99 |13.78 |1.79 |sick1 | |patient2 |13.78 |20.41 |6.63 |healthy | |... |... |... |... |... | |patient2 |90.8 |90.87 |0.07175 |sick1 | |patient2 |90.87 |106 |15.15 |healthy | |patient2 |106 |106 |0 |death | ::: ::: ::: @cr-Rmodel2result With the simple Healthy-Sick-Dead model built, let's now turn to outcome estimation. [@cr-inputs2]{highlight="11-15"} Recall that earlier, we included cost and utility weights in the inputs. [@cr-desrun2]{highlight="12-13"} Outcome estimation takes place after the model has run all patients. We do it by simply calculating and adding **cost** and **QALY** columns to the model output. [@cr-desrun2] We'll now define two functions, `cost_arrivals()` and `qaly_arrivals()` that take care of this process. [@cr-desrun2]{highlight="12-13"} These functions will be tucked into the very end of the `des_run()` function we defined that runs the simulation model. :::{#cr-desrun2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} des_run <- function(inputs) { env <<- simmer("SickSicker") traj <- des(env, inputs) env |> create_counters(counters) |> add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, inputs$N)), mon=2) |> run(inputs$horizon+1/365) |> # Simulate just past horizon (in years) wrap() get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T) |> cost_arrivals(inputs) |> qaly_arrivals(inputs) } ``` ::: ::: @cr-costarrivals2 The function `cost_arrivals()` takes as its inputs the trajectory ("arrivals") as well as the model inputs, which contains information on costs, utility weights, etc. ::: {.cell messages='false'} ::: :::{#cr-costarrivals2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} cost_arrivals <- function(arrivals, inputs) { arrivals$cost <- 0 # Undiscounted costs are 0 to begin arrivals$dcost <- 0 # Discounted costs are 0 to begin selector = arrivals$resource == 'healthy' arrivals$cost[selector] <- inputs$c.H * (arrivals$end_time[selector] - arrivals$start_time[selector]) arrivals$dcost[selector] <- discount_value(inputs$c.H, arrivals$start_time[selector], arrivals$end_time[selector], annual_rate = inputs$d.r) selector = arrivals$resource == 'sick1' arrivals$cost[selector] <- inputs$c.S1 * (arrivals$end_time[selector] - arrivals$start_time[selector]) arrivals$dcost[selector] <- discount_value(inputs$c.S1, arrivals$start_time[selector], arrivals$end_time[selector], annual_rate = inputs$d.r) arrivals } ``` ::: ::: @cr-costarrivalsresulth2 The table here shows partial trajectory ("arrivals") information for a single patient; we saw this patient's trajetory a bit earlier. [@cr-costarrivals2]{highlight="3"} Let's focus first on undiscounted costs, which start off as zero. [@cr-costarrivals2]{highlight="6"} We first select all time periods where the patient is in the [**healthy**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"} state. [@cr-costarrivals2]{highlight="7-8"} We next apply the cost parameter to the total time spent in the [**healthy**]{style="color:#6A6599FF"} state, which is `end_time` - `start_time` @cr-costarrivalsresulth2b The table shows the net result. The selected rows are highlighted in green, and we can see that the cost for each interval as been calculated. :::{#cr-costarrivalsresulth2} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
name start_time end_time resource
patient2 0 11.99 healthy
patient2 11.99 13.78 sick1
patient2 13.78 20.41 healthy
... ... ... ...
patient2 90.8 90.87 sick1
patient2 90.87 106 healthy
patient2 106 106 death
````` ::: ::: ::: :::{#cr-costarrivalsresulth2b} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
name start_time end_time resource cost
patient2 0 11.99 healthy 23980
patient2 11.99 13.78 sick1 0
patient2 13.78 20.41 healthy 13260
... ... ... ... ...
patient2 90.8 90.87 sick1 0
patient2 90.87 106 healthy 30290
patient2 106 106 death 0
````` ::: ::: ::: [@cr-costarrivals2]{highlight="12-14"} We repeat the same process for the **sick** health state. [@cr-costarrivalsresults2]{highlight="12-14"} We repeat the same process for the **sick** health state. :::{#cr-costarrivalsresults2} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
name start_time end_time resource cost
patient2 0 11.99 healthy 23980
patient2 11.99 13.78 sick1 3580
patient2 13.78 20.41 healthy 13260
... ... ... ... ...
patient2 90.8 90.87 sick1 143.5
patient2 90.87 106 healthy 30290
patient2 106 106 death NA
````` ::: ::: ::: @cr-costarrivalsresults2c One nice feature of the DES trajectory is that it is easy to assign one-time costs. @cr-costarrivalsresults2c For example, suppose there is a one-time cost of end-of-life care. We could simply add this at the time of death. :::{#cr-costarrivalsresults2c} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
name start_time end_time resource cost
patient2 0 11.99 healthy 23980
patient2 11.99 13.78 sick1 3580
patient2 13.78 20.41 healthy 13260
... ... ... ... ...
patient2 90.8 90.87 sick1 143.5
patient2 90.87 106 healthy 30290
patient2 106 106 death NA
````` ::: ::: ::: [@cr-costarrivals2]{highlight="4,9,10,11,16,17,18"} Let's now discuss discounting in DES model outputs. @cr-discount We have created a helper function `discount_value()` that takes care of continuous-time discounting for you. @cr-discount Many approaches use the power definition of discounting, which in R utilises “^” operator. This limits the numerical stable range of the function. @cr-discount Our function uses the exponential formulation with a greater numerical stability. The function also does point discounting or time period (i.e., integrated area) discounting. :::{#cr-discount} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} discount_value <- function(value, t_A, t_B=NULL, annual_rate=0.03, scale=1) { # Scale to time step if(scale != 1) { t_A <- t_A / scale if(!is.null(t_B)) t_B <- t_B / scale } # Convert discount to continuous exponential rate r <- -log(1+annual_rate) if(is.null(t_B)) { # Point estimate at t_B value*exp(r*t_A) } else { # Analytic integral of curve (value/r)*(exp(r*t_B)-exp(r*t_A)) } } ``` ::: ::: @cr-discountex For example, suppose we want to discount the value of 1, which occurs at *precisely* one year in the future. For example, this could be a one-time treatment cost. :::{#cr-discountex} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} discount_value( value = 1, t_A = 1, annual_rate = 0.03 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9708738 ``` ::: ::: ::: @cr-discountex2 Now suppose we want to discount the value 1 over the time period $t=0$ to $t=1$. For example, this type of discounting would apply for time spent in a health state. :::{#cr-discountex2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} discount_value( value = 1, t_A = 0, t_B = 1, annual_rate = 0.03 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9853651 ``` ::: ::: ::: [@cr-costarrivals2]{highlight="9,10,11,16,17,18"} Our cost calculation approach applies the `discount_value()` function to all time periods to calculate discounted costs. @cr-qalyarrivals2 We define a similar `qaly_arrivals()` function to calculate quality of life based on utility weights. [@cr-qalyarrivals2]{highlight="8,17"} The only major difference is that we multiply time in each health state with its corresponding utility weight. :::{#cr-qalyarrivals2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} qaly_arrivals <- function(arrivals, inputs) { arrivals$qaly <- 0 # No qaly yet arrivals$dqaly <- 0 # No discounted qaly either selector <- arrivals$resource == 'healthy' arrivals$qaly[selector] <- inputs$u.H* (arrivals$end_time[selector] - arrivals$start_time[selector]) arrivals$dqaly[selector] <- discount_value(inputs$u.H, arrivals$start_time[selector], arrivals$end_time[selector],annual_rate = inputs$d.r) selector <- arrivals$resource == 'sick1' arrivals$qaly[selector] <- inputs$u.S1* (arrivals$end_time[selector] - arrivals$start_time[selector]) arrivals$dqaly[selector] <- discount_value(inputs$u.S1, arrivals$start_time[selector], arrivals$end_time[selector],annual_rate = inputs$d.r) arrivals } ``` ::: ::: :::
